cells.tense: Right now you're holding the shape of this in view — what's growing, what's stalled — and your hands are steady on it.
cells.ask: Offer one thing you've been keeping back, and let the finished work be visible as finished.
cells.core:
You can see what needs feeding and what needs leaving alone, in the same glance, and the people near this are steadier for it. This isn't force and it isn't drift — it's a hand on something alive until the thing can hold itself. Keeping watch like that is a job you're doing well, and it shows in how little of it needs your hands anymore.

What's still open is whether the finished part gets to be seen. Letting a completion land, and handing over one more thing than feels entirely safe, is where you're free to go next. The room to start the next thing comes open because the last one is standing on its own.

cells.tense: You're leaning toward a version of this that hasn't happened yet, living a few steps past where anything actually is.
cells.ask: Finish one small piece today — the page, the drawer, the email — and stop when it's done, without planning its effect.
cells.core:
You can picture the whole outcome months out, and that picture is real enough to move on — but the picturing has started to run ahead of your hands. Unfinished things get resolved in your head before they're resolved on the ground, and the care that used to be patient is now steering. There's a healthier shape of this where the picture stays a picture and your hands stay with what's here.

One piece, finished, and then stop — no solving past the edge of what's visible. What you get back is the ease of having closed something without having managed what comes next.

cells.tense: You're standing a few steps back from the whole picture, and it's been a while since your own read of it carried weight with you.
cells.ask: Write one page — the thing you're tending, both sides of it, no conclusion — and mail it to someone who has kept something like it alive before.
cells.core:
You still notice how the pieces fit — you can read a room and a timeline at once — but your own read isn't landing anywhere it counts, so half-made things pile up and decisions wait. What's quiet isn't the eye. It's the hand behind it.

The way forward is small and physical: one page, both sides of what you're tending, no tidy ending, sent to a person who has kept something alive before. You don't have to believe it's good and you don't have to know where it's going. Sending it teaches you which of your reads still hold under daylight. Your own read comes back to you in someone else's words.

cells.tense: You're already keeping this going and already reading how it's turning, and it's going down as what's happening rather than what you're doing.
cells.ask: Pick one piece of this you've been calling the situation or the group's doing, and say out loud, plainly, that you're the one who has kept it going.
cells.core:
There's a steady shape to what you do here when it's working: you take in the whole picture, you keep the thing alive without fussing at it, and the people around you are calmer for it. Keeping something together like that is real work, and it gets easier once the one doing it is visible.

The gap isn't in your hands. It's in the accounting — a piece of this bearing your fingerprints is going down as nobody's, or as the wind's. Naming one piece as yours, in plain words, settles the record and lightens what you carry. What gets handed back is a truer picture of where your effort actually landed.

attempts.check: The risk is implying this person has already seen the whole pattern and simply hasn't said so, which the record does not establish; a reader could say 'I don't see the whole of anything, I just have a hunch'. The ask survives being wrong either way: drawing the one page that carries both sides of what is being tended is useful whether or not my read of their steadiness is accurate. The line that serves the writer more than the reader would be any sentence that names a feeling the record doesn't know — 'holding space without clutching' is the kind of phrase to avoid.

attempts.check: The unsupported claim running through all four is that the person is already seeing the whole pattern steadily — the record gives the capacity in the seat, not a report on their life, so each core has to narrow to what tending-under-recognition actually entails and let the person say no. A reader could reasonably say 'I don't see any whole thing, I just handle what's in front of me,' and the asks survive that: writing the state of a kept thing, or finishing one small piece, teaches something whether or not the read lands. The sentence serving the writer most was 'I don't have to know it's good yet. You just have to send it' — a line that admires its own cadence rather than the person's hand — so it's gone, and completion and visibility now do the work instead.
